item.title: He Was in Charge of Cornell’s ‘Jane Doe’ Case. Until He Wasn’t.
item.description:
It was around 4:30 p.m. on Oct. 1 when an acquaintance told Matthew Van Houten that someone from Gov. Kathy Hochul’s office was looking for his phone number. Was it OK to share it, the person asked. He said yes.

By 6 p.m., the governor hadn’t called and Mr. Van Houten, a district attorney in upstate New York, was getting ready to be questioned by local lawmakers about how he had handled a woman’s allegation that she had been sexually assaulted at a Cornell University fraternity house two years ago. At the time, Mr. Van Houten had decided not to bring charges.

That decision went mostly unnoticed outside of Cornell’s home in Ithaca, N.Y., until September, when the woman, known as Jane Doe, sued the school, her sorority, the fraternity and seven men. Now the whole country was paying attention.

As Mr. Van Houten fielded the lawmakers’ questions, he received a phone call — then a text when he didn’t answer — from someone in the governor’s office. He texted back, he recalled, saying that he couldn’t talk at the moment but would call after his meeting with the Tompkins County Legislature.

He didn’t need to. At 7:57 p.m., Mr. Van Houten received a text reply: The governor was going to announce that the state attorney general’s office was taking over the investigation of the woman’s allegation. About 10 minutes later, Ms. Hochul posted on X that she had “lost faith” in Mr. Van Houten and was removing him from the case.

The chair of the Legislature read the governor’s post aloud.

Sitting behind a large wooden desk in his office at the Tompkins County courthouse last month, Mr. Van Houten reflected on what he said was one of the most difficult months of his life.

For many, this case has formed their opinion of him. Some have demanded he resign.

“I’m not going to resign,” he said.

Nestled in the Finger Lakes region of upstate New York, Tompkins County is home to about 105,000 people.

Like many district attorneys in small and rural counties across the country, Mr. Van Houten personally prosecutes cases. His office, which has eight other attorneys, gets between 1,600 and 2,000 cases a year. Mr. Van Houten said he handles about 80 of them himself.

In 2024 came the case of Jane Doe. That November, about three weeks after the night at the fraternity house, the woman reported her accusations of sexual assault and coerced drug use at Chi Phi to the Cornell University Police Department. On Nov. 25, an investigator who took a statement from her filed a document reporting that the district attorney’s office reviewed her statement and determined that “criminal charges would not be pursued.”

But with the woman’s lawsuit this year came public pressure to reopen the investigation. As the criticism mounted, Mr. Van Houten appeared on national television and released a nine-page statement that said the evidence had not supported bringing charges.

The statement, said Anna Kelles, a Democratic state assemblywoman whose district covers Tompkins, “landed, I think, very differently than maybe he was hoping it would land for people.”

Ms. Kelles said she heard from several women who felt that Mr. Van Houten’s statement was too focused on justifying his actions. The move troubled many of her constituents who had survived sexual assaults, she said, including herself.

For days, Mr. Van Houten insisted to reporters that he made the right decision but said he would reopen the investigation. Then Ms. Hochul removed him from the case.

In the weeks that followed, a bag of feces was mailed to his home. Emails and calls threatening him and his staff came in droves. Then, there were the messages telling him someone should assault his daughter. Those threats shook him so badly he removed her photos from his office so her image would not be visible when he was being interviewed on television.

The County Legislature ordered a review of how his office handles reports of sexual assault.

Mr. Van Houten said his office is contending with “a lot of distrust” based on a single case.

“The body of work that we have established over 10 years should not be judged on the social media evaluation of this case,” he said.

Mr. Van Houten has spent most of his life in and around Tompkins County. He was raised in a neighboring county and graduated from a high school in Tompkins. He attended the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, served in the Army and graduated from Albany Law School in 1995.

He returned home to enter private practice for about 17 years, and became the chief executive of USA Team Handball, a sport he played at West Point, in 2012.

After briefly moving to Colorado, Mr. Van Houten returned to Tompkins County around 2014 and resumed his work as a defense lawyer and in family court. Two years later, he won the office of the county’s top prosecutor in an uncontested general election after a heated Democratic primary. He took the helm in January 2017.

Now in his third term in a county where Democrats outnumber Republicans by about three to one, Mr. Van Houten said he has focused on reducing the number of cases that end up in court. “I think it’s better to help somebody than to incarcerate them,” he said.

He checks the county’s jail population weekly, if not daily, he said, “to make sure that nobody’s in the jail who shouldn’t be there.” He was on the committee that launched the county’s mental health court.

He became known in the region, and across the state, as a more progressive prosecutor, according to several local lawmakers. But his first term was also marked by controversy.

One early morning in April 2019, as people spilled from bars into a public square known as the Ithaca Commons, an argument erupted, resulting in a fight. It ended when the police arrested two Black people — a man and a woman — and charged them with disorderly conduct, among other crimes.

There were protests and calls for the charges to be dropped. Mr. Van Houten’s office took the man to trial, where he was acquitted, and a judge eventually dismissed the charges against the woman. (A federal lawsuit stemming from the incident was dismissed.)

For Mr. Van Houten, the episode was a learning moment, he said.

“There are a lot of people trying to tell me how the case should be handled,” he said. “And I would still listen to people, but I need to stick with my gut more.”

On Sept. 28, overwhelmed by media requests with no one on staff to handle them, Mr. Van Houten released his statement on the Cornell case, including portions of the woman’s statement to the police.

“I wanted people to understand the process we went through and the law that we applied,” Mr. Van Houten said. “That we did believe her. We weren’t trying to victim blame her or bash her.”

But to Irene Weiser, a county legislator, one of the most glaring problems in the case was that Mr. Van Houten said his office did not communicate directly with the woman before deciding not to pursue charges.

Mr. Van Houten said he is now requiring his assistant district attorneys to ask to meet with each person who reports a sexual assault, though he said meeting with Jane Doe would not have changed his decision at that time. But it might have put his office in a better position to respond to the criticism now, he said.

The county is also instituting changes. The sheriff’s department unveiled a proposal last month to create a new Special Victims Unit staffed with deputies and an assistant district attorney. The plan, which is also spearheaded by some lawmakers, is one Mr. Van Houten said he supports and has already been proposed to the governor.

But the decisions that he made in 2024 were not flippant ones, Mr. Van Houten said in an interview.

“They were not decisions that were made without a thoughtful analysis of the law,” he said. “So that’s the comfort I have.”

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: How 6 Americans Under 40 Are Trying to Build a Retirement Stash
item.description:
The old paradigm of getting a steady job, buying a home by age 30 — or ever — and building a career with one employer has all but crumbled.

But in Americans’ personal finances, one thing hasn’t changed: the need to save for retirement. Because they are juggling student loan debts and health care costs, many younger workers find doing that almost impossible. Yet some millennials and members of Generation Z are finding ways to save, even if that means making hard choices or rejecting experts’ advice.

The New York Times spoke with six adults under 40, who are all single and don’t have children, about their financial priorities and their methods of saving and investing for their later years.

“If your priorities look different from people that are older in your life, trust your instincts to take a different path.”

Zayda Slabbekoorn

Zayda Slabbekoorn has two big financial goals: save for retirement and build an emergency fund. She invests 5 percent of her salary in a 401(k) plan at work, but right now the emergency fund is taking the front seat.

So she aims to save $10,000 in cash in case she’s laid off as an editorial strategist or decides to move away from Grand Rapids, Mich.

Each month, $600 is automatically deducted from her paycheck and put into a high-yield savings account toward that emergency fund. Any excess — typically about $100 a month — also goes there. “I want to feel like I have control over my financial situation as much as possible,” she said. At a previous job, Ms. Slabbekoorn, 24, put 8 percent into her 401(k) and received an employer match. She no longer has a match, and doesn’t feel as comfortable putting that much in a retirement plan without it.

“I feel like my money is better located in a savings account that I can access without having to take any kind of penalty” for withdrawing it, she said.

Once she builds the emergency fund, Ms. Slabbekoorn said, she will consider bumping up her retirement savings and paying down her student loan debt more aggressively — at the moment, she is paying the minimum $700 monthly on an $80,000 balance. She freelances to make extra money.

Her father gives her advice, but it doesn’t always align with her goals, she said. When her parents were her age, they were married with a mortgage and plans for a family. But she isn’t sketching out that kind of future and has stopped comparing herself with her parents.

“I feel like I’m controlling the things I can control, and there’s not much more I can do.”

Rayshaw Whitford

Rayshaw Whitford, 36, bought a house in Woodbridge, Conn., this year. His mortgage consumes 25 percent of his gross income, and he no longer has student loan debt, having paid it off several years after college, so he’s in a position to save.

Mr. Whitford maxes out his 401(k) each year and receives a match from the nonprofit foundation where he is an operations director, but he didn’t start saving there until he was 29, which he regrets.

“My first job, where I was making good money, I didn’t know enough to start saving,” said Mr. Whitford, who hadn’t thought he would stay at the company long enough to become vested in its plan. “So I thought, why put money into what I wouldn’t have access to until later?” he said. Now, he budgets for his contribution.

He wants to save $1.5 million by age 55. Yet he wonders if it will be enough, and he isn’t confident Social Security and Medicare will be there for him.

“Gen Z has a very nonlinear view of what financial security looks like.”

Amrita Bhasin

Amrita Bhasin, 25, has been using her father’s financial advice since he insisted she open a Roth individual retirement account at 14, when she got her first summer job. Now, she’s an entrepreneur, having co-founded a supply chain software company in San Francisco. At his urging, last November Ms. Bhasin set up a 401(k) plan for the small company and its workers, and she maxes out her own contribution. She’s also the only one using it.

Ms. Bhasin follows her father’s guidance, but she believes that career paths today are less predictable and that Gen Z is likely to take a different financial path than previous generations did.

“Many people feel like they’re not going to be able to afford to buy a house like the one that they grew up in,” Ms. Bhasin said. She questions what financial stability will look like for her generation.

Maxing out a 401(k) can require a level of sacrifice that is difficult for the average person, Ms. Bhasin said. To shore up her finances, she supplements her income with freelance work and, for the past several years, has made an annual plan for spending on vacations, clothes and experiences. “I usually stay pretty close to my annual budget,” she said.

“Growing up, my dad and I used to talk about retirement planning and being strategic with the things we do.”

Jabari Washington

Jabari Washington, 25, received a full scholarship to college to study math and actuarial science, graduating with no student loan debt. He also worked throughout school, including at a well-paying internship. That allowed him to save enough to buy a house in Bloomington-Normal, Ill., even before graduating in May 2023. Last year, he bought a second house in town.

It helps, he said, that housing prices where he lives are reasonable (according to Zillow, the average home there is about $270,000, lower than the national average). Mr. Washington lives in one of the houses with roommates who pay rent and rents the other house.

How does he manage to do that while also saving separately for retirement? Mr. Washington’s internship led to a career as an actuary, in which he earns six figures. When it comes to retirement savings, he takes a traditional route: He puts 6 percent in a 401(k), receiving a 3 percent employer match.

He also saves $4,400 a year in a health savings account and has three brokerage accounts, two of which he opened in college. One of those accounts holds the money he tithes to his church — 10 percent of his salary. “I’m trying to wean myself off of keeping everything for myself,” Mr. Washington said.

“I don’t really understand anything about pensions, to be fully transparent, and I’ve never stayed at a job for five years.”

Alexa Hayes

Alexa Hayes, a graphic designer, prefers having liquid assets to locking up her savings in a workplace plan, so she invests in the stock market directly using a brokerage account. She also considers her Washington, D.C., apartment, which she owns (thanks partly to an inheritance), to be a big piece of her retirement plan. “It’s paid off so, in theory, I can sell it for profit and then invest that income,” she said.

Last year, when Ms. Hayes, 38, lost her federal contractor job, she had to sell $2,000 in stock and use all her cash savings of $25,000 to pay bills while she searched for another role. The hunt took 10 months, and her longstanding freelance work helped.

“It was dire straits, and having that access to money felt much safer than tucking it away in a 401(k),” she said. (She did not qualify for unemployment.)

While out of work, Ms. Hayes deferred payments on the $60,000 she owes in student loans, and since October, has been required to make monthly student loan payments of $665. The interest is a burden, she said. “The daily accrual on student loans is so suffocating, it feels like you are chipping away at a mountain that continues to grow.”

Ms. Hayes was hired at a nonprofit that offers a pension and a 403(b), which is similar to a 401(k). She will be fully vested in the pension in five years and admits she doesn’t fully understand how it works. She doesn’t plan to contribute to the 403(b) this year or next.

“When you only pay the minimum, you’re going to be absolutely destroyed by interest.”

Chase Cooper

For the last two years, Chase Cooper, 38, has worked overtime every week so he can keep saving for retirement and have money to socialize with friends and take vacations. He is saving 6 percent of his salary in a 401(k) with an employer match, and last year he began contributing the maximum to a Roth I.R.A.

Mr. Cooper said he didn’t start saving for retirement right away. “I feel like I’m late to the party,” he said.

The reason: Mr. Cooper started his career as a professional pianist, taking “whatever would pay,” but his income was low — so he switched careers and became a travel nurse. He began contributing 5 percent of his income to a 403(b) plan at his first nursing job and knew he needed three years of continuous service to be vested in it — but he quit too soon and forfeited the employer match portion.

“It felt like the rug was pulled out from under me,” said Mr. Cooper, who is currently working in Omaha. Home base is Birmingham, Ala.

He does have $51,000 in student loans to clear, and pays $1,000 toward them each month. Mr. Cooper pays more than the required minimum of $750 so he can stay ahead of the interest.

Health insurance premiums have also been a big expense. Until recently, Mr. Cooper paid $900 a month for a Blue Cross plan from the Affordable Care Act marketplace. He decided to change that, and opted into his employer’s health care plan, which lowers his monthly premiums to $600.

“I’m thinking of putting the savings into investments, but I honestly haven’t made up my mind yet,” he said.

item.title: What Does It Actually Mean to Write ‘Like a Human’?
item.description:
Suddenly, everyone’s become an A.I. detective.

We now have checklists of the supposed telltale signs that something was written by a chatbot. There are companies that claim their detection software can catch it for you. Paranoia. Finger-pointing. Witch hunts.

Then last year, that cloud of suspicion fell on Marcus Olang’.

After Olang’, a writer in Nairobi, Kenya, was accused of sounding like ChatGPT, he wondered: What does it mean to write like a robot in the first place?

In the Opinion Video above, Olang’ argues that the frenzy over catching A.I. writing tells us a deeper, older story. It’s not actually about technology, but about what it means to sound, and be, human — how that definition has changed throughout history, and who it leaves behind.

Below is an edited transcript of this video. We recommend watching it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the video player above.

Marcus Olang’: Last year, I sent off a project proposal I’d worked on for days. Proper days. And then the reply came back: Could you do a rewrite with a more human touch? It sounds a little like it was written by ChatGPT.

A more human touch. A more human touch.

It’s a sentence that got me wondering: What does it actually mean to sound like a robot? And what does it mean to sound like a human?

Here’s the thing, though: I don’t write like ChatGPT — ChatGPT writes like me. Or more accurately, it writes like the millions of us around the world who were taught a very specific kind of English — taught to polish our thoughts into this exact same shape. Let me explain.

My formal writing journey started in Mrs. Amollo’s English classroom in Nairobi, Kenya, when I was about 9. Mrs. Amollo spoke in a careful, considered accent: the Queen’s English, a colonial relic, an inheritance of sorts. And this English, we learned, had rules.

Show off your vocabulary: You never just walked; you strode purposefully. You didn’t just see a thing; you beheld a magnificent spectacle.

Reach for a simile in every paragraph: Your heart never raced; it pounded like a drum. Purity, we were told, was “as white as snow” — this, in a country that only ever sees snow atop Mt. Kenya. And not many people see the top of Mt. Kenya.

Make your points in threes — always in threes. A beginning, a conflict, a moral. The character, the motivation, the growth. Balanced, weighted, complete.

Additionally, you never let a thought merely stand on its own. Therefore, you brace it with a transition. Consequently, your reader is never left wondering where you’re headed.

And the highest art of them all: the contrasting parallel. Say a thing by naming its opposite. It’s not the size of the dog in the fight; it’s the size of the fight in the dog. It’s not what you know; it’s who you know. It is not this; it’s that.

And you bring it all together in the long sentence — the longer, the better. Every thought telegraphed, announced and delivered, the whole procession rolling on in one measured breath until it arrives — finally, gracefully, completely — at its full stop.

This was the formula to become a proper writer — a proper human writer. If you studied English in a former British colony or territory, all of this may sound familiar to you.

All those lessons built to one moment: the national exam at the end of primary school. Forty minutes to write a single original story by hand on a double-sided A4 paper. An examinable demonstration of your understanding of all of those rules. And riding on it: your chance at a place in a good high school, then a good university, then a good career. Which is to say, the rest of your life.

And then ——

Archival news clip: A new artificial intelligence program called ChatGPT.

Archival news clip: ChatGPT.

Archival news clip: Humanlike writing ability.

Archival news clip: Humanlike text.

Archival news clip: But with more humanlike features.

Somebody feeds this machine what exactly? A vast archive of human language including, yes, centuries of formal, published English. The books, the law, the scientific journals, the Shakespeare, the Scripture — the same texts that built the register Mrs. Amollo drilled into us. And this machine suddenly comes out the other side sounding like the best student Mrs. Amollo ever had. A machine that suddenly sounds like me.

Social media clip: Ten obvious signs you’re using A.I. for writing.

Social media clip: Very easy telltale signs that something was written by ChatGPT.

Podcast clip: Longer sentences, paragraphs are rarely interrupted with short, punchy statements.

Social media clip: The rule of three, or listicles when it doesn’t need to be there.

Social media clip: Weird transitions like “moreover.”

Social media clip: Instead of saying, “This building is a gallery,” it says, “This building serves as a gallery.”

Social media clip: The classic “It’s not about X, it’s about Y” line.

Podcast clip: I just saw this referred to as “The DiGiorno Construct.”

Clip of archival DiGiorno Pizza ad: It’s not delivery. It’s DiGiorno.

Social media clip: Most people just don’t speak or write like that.

Social media clip: If this seems like you, it might be time to put down the A.I. and read a book.

A while back, a big Silicon Valley investor announced that if your email included the word “delve,” then a robot wrote it. Nobody real talks or writes like that, was basically his point.

And to that, the whole British Commonwealth — from Lagos to Nairobi to Mumbai — looked over the tops of their glasses and went: My brother in Christ, “delve” is just English. It’s the English we were taught. We shan’t be judged because we read more English than you, please.

But while we’re here, let’s talk about “delve.” Or, in the original Old English, “delfan,” which means “to dig.” Centuries later, Shakespeare put it in “Hamlet”: “But I will delve one yard below their mines.”

Richard Burton as Hamlet on Broadway, 1964: But I will delve one yard below their mines.

David Tennant as Hamlet, Royal Shakespeare Company, 2008: Delve one yard below their mines / And blow them at the moon.

And that very English made its way onto a ship to my part of the world on the tongue of the missionary. And that missionary passed it on to the head teacher — part of the proper English we were told to master if we wanted to be considered educated, to be considered civilized, to be considered human.

And while written English in America or Britain kept evolving, what we were taught in our classrooms didn’t. Even after Kenya’s independence, these lessons were cyclically imposed, repeatedly drilled, then calcified. They remained entrenched, frozen in time.

We internalized them so thoroughly that “delve” — a word that now sounds archaic to American or British ears — stayed perfectly ordinary in Lagos and Nairobi. Boring, even; a word you’d casually, nonchalantly throw into Pages 2, 12 or 22 of a report.

So how did this everyday word in Nairobi become a chatbot’s biggest tell? Well, maybe it’s because when A.I. companies needed cheap labor to help teach their new machines how to distinguish between “good” and “bad” writing, guess who they hired? Data workers in Kenya, for a couple of dollars an hour.

Picture it: Someone in Nairobi sits in front of two sample answers and picks the one that looks like the good writing they were taught — the one that uses words like “delve” — a couple of hundred times a day. Then, a couple of years later, a man in California looks at it and says: Yep, that’s for sure a robot word. And it’s not just some tech bro posting on Twitter. (I refuse to call it X.)

When researchers tested A.I.-detection software on essays written by nonnative English speakers, the software incorrectly flagged more than half as A.I.-generated. Now, guess how many essays by American students got the this-is-human stamp of approval? Go on, guess. Almost all of them. And the irony is there’s now a whole industry built on selling us a solution.

Social media clip: Just come over to StealthGPT and go to their A.I. humanizer.

Social media clip: Click “humanize” and Humbot will do all the work for you.

That’s right. A website — another A.I. tool — that says it will help you “humanize” your writing and pass A.I. detection.

Social media clip: Just paste in your text, click “humanize,” and it rewrites your text with more natural words and sentences.

So that’s the whole loop. A classroom the British Empire built teaches and conditions us to write a certain way. A machine learns that way — partly taught by us. A second machine gets built to catch the first one, often flagging the exact features that were drilled into us.

And now we’re sold a new machine — a “humanizer” machine — to rough our English back up. Chopping up a long sentence here, dropping a “furthermore” there, so the previous machine and its believers can finally accept that we’re human.

Do you see how the goal posts keep moving?

We spend a decade and a half mastering formal English to be taken seriously in a world that needs convincing. And now that we’ve succeeded? The rules change — again. Now “human” means the slang — the loose, the casual, the imperfect. The fluid, evolving language of modern-day London and Los Angeles. The perfect is no longer “human” — the error is.

So “human” was never a real place we were meant to reach. It’s just the word for wherever we happen not to be. Which tells us that this — the whole panic over catching A.I. — was never just about technology. Perhaps it’s about how we define what “human” is in the first place.

No robots were used in the making of this video. The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft claiming copyright infringement. The companies have denied those claims.
